content: 1. Children with congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection who do not exhibit neurological symptoms within the first year of life are unlikely to develop neurodevelopmental or intellectual impairments later in life. It is widely accepted that neurological sequelae of congenital CMV infection do not typically manifest after the age of two years. 2. In developing recommendations for the follow-up of children in areas with Zika virus transmission, the guideline development group considered existing WHO guidelines for neurodevelopmental follow-up, as well as auditory and ophthalmologic screening protocols. 3. Infants with congenital Zika virus syndrome should undergo follow-up evaluations at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months of age. Additional follow-up should be provided if complications arise. Beyond 24 months, further follow-up will depend on the child’s condition and specific needs. 4. At each follow-up visit, head circumference should be measured to monitor postnatal brain growth. For term neonates, the WHO Child Growth Standards (CGS) should be used to interpret head circumference measurements. For preterm neonates, the INTERGROWTH-21st postnatal growth standards should be used until 64 weeks postmenstrual age, after which the WHO CGS should be applied. 5. Developmental and neurological assessments should be conducted with active caregiver involvement to identify developmental delays and neurological abnormalities, including epilepsy, movement disorders, postural issues, and swallowing difficulties. 6. Hearing should be screened within the first month of life, ideally before hospital discharge. Further audiological evaluations and services should follow WHO guidelines for newborn and infant hearing screening, as well as the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing’s position statement. 7. Comprehensive ophthalmological assessments should be performed to evaluate vision and detect any abnormalities. 8. The health and well-being of families and caregivers, including their psychological well-being, should be assessed and supported. 9. Infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection during pregnancy, even in the absence of microcephaly or disproportionately small head size relative to the face, should be monitored for signs of neurodevelopmental abnormalities. These include feeding difficulties, hearing or vision problems, and poor head growth. Follow-up visits should occur at 3, 9, and 24 months of age at a minimum. 10. Families and caregivers should receive psychosocial support and parenting advice to help them manage the challenges associated with caring for affected infants. 11. Neonates should have their head circumference measured within the first 24 hours of life. For term neonates, the WHO Child Growth Standards for size at birth should be used, while for preterm neonates, the INTERGROWTH-21st standards for gestational age and sex should be applied. 12. Mothers should be asked about clinical signs and symptoms of Zika virus infection during pregnancy, including laboratory confirmation and the timing of the possible infection (first, mid, or final trimester). 13. Neonates should be examined for craniofacial disproportion, where the head appears disproportionately small relative to the face. 14. In neonates with congenital microcephaly or disproportionately small head size, a full history, physical examination, and neurological assessment, including hearing and vision evaluations, should be performed to detect additional abnormalities potentially associated with Zika virus infection. 15. Neuroimaging should be performed in neonates with head circumference measurements below -2 standard deviations (SD) but above -3 SD, or in cases of disproportionately small head size, if Zika virus infection is suspected in the mother during pregnancy or if neurological signs or symptoms are present. 16. For neonates with head circumference below -3 SD, neuroimaging should be conducted unless there is a strong indication of a genetic or environmental cause of microcephaly. 17. When neuroimaging is indicated, either computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used. CT is sufficient to identify findings suggestive of congenital Zika virus syndrome, while MRI may provide additional detail and help diagnose other conditions. If CT or MRI is unavailable, cranial ultrasound can be performed if the anterior fontanelle is adequately sized. 18. Serological testing for TORCH infections should be performed in neonates with congenital microcephaly, disproportionately small head size, or suspected Zika virus infection in the mother during pregnancy, or if neurological signs or symptoms are present. 19. The role of serological and virological testing for Zika virus in neonates should be evaluated based on further data regarding sensitivity, specificity, and cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses. 20. Families of neonates with congenital Zika syndrome should be informed about the diagnosis and provided with guidance on management and prognosis. 21. Psychosocial support and advice should be offered to families of neonates with congenital Zika virus syndrome, as outlined in WHO interim guidance on psychosocial support for families affected by microcephaly and other neurological complications in the context of Zika virus. 22. Infants with congenital Zika virus syndrome should receive comprehensive neurodevelopmental assessments, and supportive therapies should be implemented to address any identified difficulties, such as irritability, seizures, swallowing difficulties, early-onset spasticity, and hip dysplasia. 23. Multidisciplinary approaches should be adopted to provide early interventions and support, promote neurodevelopment, prevent contractures, and manage early complications, as outlined in WHO’s mental health gap action programme (mhGAP) and community-based rehabilitation guidelines. 24. A systematic search of evidence was conducted to inform these guidelines, including literature on microcephaly, congenital infections, and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Relevant articles were reviewed, and evidence summaries were developed to guide recommendations. 25. A guideline development group (GDG) was established, comprising experts in microcephaly, pediatric neurology, neonatology, and epidemiology, including representatives from affected countries. The group met in March 2016 to finalize the recommendations. 26. Draft recommendations were reviewed by an external group to ensure scientific accuracy, feasibility, and clarity for policymakers and program staff. 27. All GDG members completed declarations of interest, and no conflicts were identified. The guideline process was coordinated by WHO departments specializing in maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health, mental health, nutrition, and reproductive health.
